group.passage: Small cuts are part of everyday life, and most of us take care of them in seconds. We simply open an adhesive bandage, peel off the paper, and press it on. About a hundred years ago, however, caring for a small wound was not so easy. The bandages of that time were large and clumsy, and it was hard to put one on without help. The handy strip we use today came from a husband who wanted to make life easier for his wife. The husband was Earle Dickson, who bought cotton for the company Johnson & Johnson. His wife, Josephine, often cut or burned her fingers while cooking. Dickson's company already made surgical tape and gauze, but it sold them as two separate products, so he decided to put them together. He stuck small pieces of clean gauze onto a long strip of tape and covered the sticky side with a stiff cloth so that the tape would not stick to itself. Now Josephine could cut off a piece and put it on by herself. When Dickson showed his idea to the company's leaders, what caught their attention was that a person could put on the bandage without anyone's help. The company began selling the product, called the Band-Aid, in 1920. However, the Band-Aid got off to a slow start: the bandages were made by hand, and only about $3,000 worth were sold in the first year. Things improved after the company handed out large numbers of free Band-Aids to groups of Boy Scouts. In 1924, machines began making them in different sizes, and in 1939 they became fully sterilized. Dickson stayed with the company and later became one of its vice presidents. The basic design of his bandage has changed very little, and more than 100 billion of them have been made. In 2017, long after his death, he was added to the National Inventors Hall of Fame. His story shows that a great invention does not always begin in a laboratory. Sometimes it begins in a kitchen, with someone who simply wants to help a person he loves.

translation_zh.text:
小傷口是日常生活的一部分，我們大多數人幾秒鐘就能處理好。我們只要打開一片 OK 繃，撕掉背紙，貼上去就好。然而大約一百年前，照顧一個小傷口可沒有這麼容易。當時的繃帶又大又笨重，沒有人幫忙很難自己包紮。我們今天使用的這種方便小貼布，來自一位想讓太太生活輕鬆一點的丈夫。
這位丈夫叫做厄爾．迪克森，他在嬌生公司負責採購棉花。他的太太約瑟芬做菜時常常割傷或燙傷手指。迪克森的公司本來就生產外科膠帶和紗布，但把它們當成兩種不同的產品分開賣，於是他決定把兩者結合起來。他把一小塊一小塊乾淨的紗布黏在一長條膠帶上，再用一塊硬布蓋住有黏性的那一面，讓膠帶不會黏在一起。這下子約瑟芬就能自己剪下一段貼上了。
迪克森把這個點子拿給公司主管看時，最吸引他們注意的是：一個人不需要別人幫忙就能貼上這種繃帶。公司在 1920 年開始販售這項產品，取名為 Band-Aid。然而，OK 繃起步並不順利：當時的繃帶是手工製作的，第一年只賣出大約 3,000 美元。後來公司把大量免費的 OK 繃發送給童軍團，情況才開始好轉。1924 年起改用機器生產不同尺寸的 OK 繃，到了 1939 年則做到完全消毒。
迪克森一直留在這家公司，後來成為副總裁之一。他設計的繃帶基本樣式幾乎沒有改變，至今已經生產了超過一千億片。2017 年，在他過世很久之後，他被列入美國國家發明家名人堂。他的故事告訴我們，偉大的發明不一定從實驗室開始。有時候，它從廚房開始，來自一個只是想幫助心愛之人的人。
